Footer.tagline:
A chess variant where time is a resource. Captures, moves, and checks all add or remove time.
Independent, free, run at cost by one person

learn.metaDescription: An interactive, minute-long tutorial: how captures, checks and tolls move time between clocks in KiriChess.
learn.playRequiresAccount: You'll need a free account to play, but a bot game is free and starts instantly, no wait and no rating on the line.
learn.stepWinWithoutMateBody: Checkmate still wins, exactly as in chess. And just like in regular chess, you win if your opponent's clock reaches zero, unless they cannot mate with what is left, which is a draw. But in KiriChess, time is a resource: captures, moves, and checks all add or remove time. You can attack their clock with captures and checks, not just wait for it to run out.
learn.stepMovingCostsTimeBody: Moving a piece costs time off your own clock, and the toll depends on which piece you pick up. The toll is charged on top of the time you already spent thinking. Move any piece and see what happens.
learn.stepCapturesStealBody: KiriChess has three capture economies: Steal, Burn, and Bounty. This board is Steal ({steal1}): capturing a piece transfers time from them to you. Try capturing the knight, or just sandbox around.
learn.stepCapturesBurnTitle: Burn: they lose, you gain nothing.
learn.stepCapturesBurnBody: This board is Burn ({burn1}). Capturing still takes time off their clock, but none of it lands on yours. Try capturing the knight, or just sandbox around.
learn.stepCapturesBountyTitle: Bounty: you gain, their clock stays put.
learn.stepCapturesBountyBody: This board is Bounty ({bounty1}). Capturing adds time to your clock, and theirs does not move. Try capturing the knight, or just sandbox around.
learn.stepCheckBody: A checking move earns the checker a small chip and costs the checked side one too, stacked on top of whatever the move already costs. Slide the rook down the open file to check the king and watch both clocks move.
learn.stepRepetitionTitle: Repeat a position, and the transfer disappears.
learn.stepRepetitionBody: Shuffle a knight out and back, on both sides. The moment the board returns to a position it has already reached once before, that move's entire transfer, toll included, is cancelled. Play all four moves: out, out, back, back.
learn.stepDoneBody: Captures shift time between the clocks (Steal, Burn or Bounty, depending on the pool), moving costs time, a check chips both clocks, and repeating a position cancels the transfer entirely. Sandbox as much as you'd like, then play a real game or read the rules for the full depth.
learn.movingCostsTimePayoff: You moved a {piece}. It cost you {cost}. {suffix}
learn.movingCostsTimePawnAside: The smallest piece has the smallest cost.
learn.movingCostsTimeQueenAside: The most powerful piece is also the most expensive to shuffle around.
learn.capturesStealCapturedPayoff: You captured a {piece}. After the move cost, you gained {gain} and they lost {loss}. A single capture, two clocks moving in opposite directions, that's Steal.
learn.capturesStealMovePayoff: That was a regular move with your {piece} costing {cost}. Try capturing to see the Steal economy in action!
learn.capturesBurnCapturedPayoff: You captured a {piece}. After the move cost, your clock nets {net} and they lost {loss}. Their time left the board and went nowhere, that's Burn.
learn.capturesBurnMovePayoff: That was a regular move with your {piece}, costing {cost}. Try capturing to see the Burn economy in action!
learn.capturesBountyCapturedPayoff: You captured a {piece}. After the move cost, you gained {gain} and their clock did not move. The time appeared on your clock and nowhere else, that's Bounty.
learn.capturesBountyMovePayoff: That was a regular move with your {piece}, costing {cost}. Try capturing to see the Bounty economy in action!
learn.stepCheckPayoff: Check! Your clock nets {gain} on that move: the toll for moving the rook, minus the chip for checking them. Their clock drops {loss}, just for being in check.
learn.stepRepetitionShufflePayoff: Move {step} of {total}: shuffling the {piece} cost {cost}, an ordinary toll.
learn.stepRepetitionNullifiedPayoff: The board is back where it already was. This move's transfer is cancelled: it would have cost {wouldBe}, but nets {actual} instead.

rules.metaDescription: How KiriChess's time economy works: captures, checks and tolls move time between clocks instead of a fixed increment.
rules.tocChanges: How it changes the way you play
rules.tocQueenCost: Why the queen's toll is discounted
rules.conceptH1: Chess, but time is a resource.
rules.changesHeading: How it changes the way you play
rules.changesPara1: The first thing that changes is that no move is free anymore. Every move costs time, so every move comes with a question: is this worth x seconds?
rules.changesPara2: The second thing is that a piece stops having only one price. A knight is worth 3 points in chess and that number never moves all game. Here the same knight has three more prices: what your opponent gets if they take it, what it costs you every time you move it, and what it can earn you if it starts giving check.
rules.changesPara3: The third one takes the longest to learn: time stops being just how you lose, and starts being something you can take from each other. Your opponent can go after your clock with checks, with trades, with a piece you hang. You have to defend it, and you can also attack theirs.
rules.changesPara4: KiriChess adds a second question to every move: what does this do to the clocks? Sometimes those two answers disagree: the objectively correct move is a trade you can't afford, or a "bad" move turns out to be right because it eats your opponent's time.
rules.changesPara5: Which is why games here don't just end the two ways they do in normal chess. You still get mates, and you still get the last-second scramble where someone's flag falls. There's a third ending: a forced flagfall. A plan that might not threaten mate or win a single pawn, but drains your opponent's time until their flag falls in a position that looks completely fine on the board.
rules.unchangedPara1: Everything from chess still applies unless this manual says otherwise: how pieces move, check, checkmate, stalemate, castling, en passant, promotion, threefold repetition, the fifty-move rule, and a draw when neither side can mate. If you can play chess, you already know most of KiriChess. This manual is the time economy layered on top that changes the decisions you make.
rules.unchangedPara2: The rules stack in a fixed order: capture economy at the base, movement toll on top of it, the check chip on top of that, and a repetition guard wrapping all three so none of them can be farmed.
rules.rulesIntro: Three rules move the clocks: captures, moves, and checks. The fourth is the protection rule, repetition, which shuts those three off if the position has already been seen, so you can't farm free time by looping.
rules.capturesIntro: Capturing a piece moves the clock. How much, and who it moves it for, depends on the pool's economy. Bigger pieces are worth more seconds.
rules.stealCardBody: Captor <gains>gains</gains>, victim <loses>loses</loses>. Time transfers from victim to captor, only winning material moves the gap.
rules.bountyCardBody: Captor <gains>gains</gains>, nobody loses. Capturing adds time; games run longer.
rules.burnCardBody: Victim <loses>loses</loses>, captor gains nothing. Even equal trades drain both clocks.
rules.captureFootnote: Values shown at base scale ({multiplier}). Rated pools apply a capture multiplier on top of these numbers, see <pools>The {poolCount} pools</pools>. En passant counts as a normal pawn capture.
rules.tollsIntro: Every move costs time off your own clock, priced by the piece you move. A queen move is expensive; the king is cheap so king activity in the endgame stays affordable.
rules.tollsNeverScaleBody: The toll table above is what you pay in every rated pool, regardless of its capture multiplier.
rules.castlingDiscountBody: Priced individually, castling would move a king ({kingToll}s) and a rook ({rookToll}s) for {unbundled}s total. Instead it's a single flat {castleCost}s fee, the same for either side, since castling is almost always a good move.
rules.zugzwangBody: In chess, being forced to move is sometimes only positionally painful. In KiriChess, you also pay for every forced move.
rules.avgMoveCostTitle: The average move costs about {avgToll} seconds
rules.avgMoveCostBody: Weighted by real-game move frequency, that's about {tollDrain} seconds of toll per player over a {movesPerPlayer}-move game. The queen and rook together make only ~{heavyMoveShare}% of all moves but pay ~{heavyTollShare}% of all toll.
rules.checkChipIntro: Delivering check in a new, non-repeated position chips {chip} seconds off the checked player and onto the checker. A check that is mate pays no chip. Double check pays {multiplier}×, a discovered attack that checks with two pieces at once steals {doubleChip}s at base. The checking move still bills its own toll, so not every check turns a profit.
rules.checkChipReadNote: The cheaper the piece delivering the check, the more profitable the attack. Because tolls and chips never scale, this table is true in every rated pool.
rules.repetitionIntro: If the position on the board has occurred earlier in the game, the move triggers no time effects at all: no capture value, no toll, and checks stop chipping. Without this guard, perpetual check would farm your opponent's clock to zero without ever improving the position.
rules.repetitionLi1: A "position" follows the official chess definition: piece placement + side to move + castling rights + en passant availability.
rules.repetitionLi2: Once a position has been seen, it is nullified for the rest of the game, you can't dodge the guard by alternating between two different repetition patterns.
rules.repetitionLi3: Threefold repetition is automatic: the instant a position occurs for the third time, the game is drawn immediately, no player action required.
rules.repetitionFootnote: In a healthy game you'll rarely notice this rule.
rules.promotionFreeBody: The promoting move pays only the ordinary pawn toll (<toll>{pawnToll}s</toll>), nothing extra for the new piece. The pawn already paid the march tolls, and the new queen is priced by Rule 1 like any other queen.
rules.promotionPricedBody: On top of the {pawnToll}s pawn toll, promoting charges {mult}× the new piece's value: <cost>{queenCost}s</cost> for a queen. Under-promotion is cheaper.
rules.enPassantBody: Treated exactly as a normal pawn capture: same economy, same <val>±{pawnCapture}s</val> at base, scaled by the pool's capture multiplier like any other capture.
rules.endingFootnote: Steal and Burn fight draws in different ways. In Steal, the player behind has to win material (or chip) to get time back, which forces contact. In Burn, the player ahead can force trades the short clock cannot afford. Bounty is the exception: captures refill instead of draining. Tolls still run in every pool, so a totally quiet game still ends on the clock.
rules.endingCheckmateDescription: Immediate win, even if the mating move's toll would have flagged you. The toll still comes off your clock. Mate is decided before the flag.
rules.endingFlagFallDescriptionWithDraw: Win, unless you hold only a king, or a king and a single bishop or knight, in which case it's a draw.
rules.endingFlagVsBareKingDescription: The flag falls, and the player who would have won holds only a king, or a king and a single bishop or knight. Draw.
rules.endingStalemateDescription: No legal move, not in check, same as classical chess. It is still a draw if that move would have flagged you.
rules.endingThreefoldDescription: Draw, no claim needed, the game ends the instant the third occurrence is reached. It outranks the flag, the same way mate does.
rules.endingTimeoutDescriptionWithDraw: Your clock hits zero. You lose, unless the opponent holds only a king, or a king and a single bishop or knight, in which case it's a draw.
rules.endingTimeoutDescriptionNoDraw: Your clock hits zero. You lose.
rules.endingFiftyMoveDescription: Fifty moves by each side with no capture and no pawn move. Draw, as in classical chess. It outranks the flag.
rules.endingInsufficientDescription: Neither side can mate. Draw, the moment the position is dead. It outranks the flag.
rules.endingAbandonedDescription: You leave the game and don't return. You lose.
rules.economyIntro: How the three economies price the same events differently, and how that changes the way you play.
rules.victoryH3: The price of victory: mate costs money
rules.victoryIntro: Delivering checkmate takes moves, and moves cost time. Approximate time costs for the basic mates:
rules.mateTableFootnote: Practical move counts vary with piece placement and defender resistance; bills are the toll cost of that many moves at base rates, not a hard guarantee.
rules.conversionBillPara: Because tolls never scale, the conversion bill is the same in every rated pool. So while playing that means you can be completely winning on the board and unable to afford the win. If you reach K+R vs K with less than {bill} seconds on your clock, you will flag mid-conversion if your opponent doesn't slip up.
rules.mateLi1: Budget your endgame before you enter it. Before liquidating into a winning ending, check whether your clock can cover the conversion bill.
rules.mateLi2: Mate in the middlegame is cheaper than mate in the endgame. A sharp, clean mating attack costs a handful of tolls; a technical grind costs a fortune.
rules.mateLi3: Know the technique, don't improvise it. The costs above assume the textbook method, driving the king to the edge with no wasted moves. If you don't convert efficiently you'll run out of time.
rules.tradeMathIntro: The three main economies price the same knight trade completely differently:
rules.tradeMathFootnote: Under Burn, an equal trade drains {equalTrade} seconds from both players, and "can I even afford to trade?" becomes a question. Under Bounty, trades inflate both clocks and games run longer the more material is captured. But your opponent might be low on time, making an equal trade disadvantageous. Under Steal, only genuine material wins matter.
rules.queenCostH3: Why the queen costs {queenToll} and not {undiscounted}
rules.queenCostPara: By raw material logic, the queen (worth a rook + bishop) "should" cost {undiscounted}s to move if the rook costs {rookToll} and the bishop {bishopToll}. She's discounted for two reasons. First, tolls are paid per move, and the queen is the most-moved piece in most attacks: linear pricing would tax attacking chess into the ground; a ten-move queen attack at Q={undiscounted} costs {tenXUndiscounted} seconds on top of the double price sacrifices already pay. Second, the check table above. At Q={queenToll}, queen checks are exactly self-financing. At Q={undiscounted} they'd be gap-negative: attacking with your queen would lose you time even while giving checks.
rules.poolsIntro: Each pool locks in a time control, an economy, and a capture multiplier (C). The multiplier scales capture transfers/burns only, tolls and chips stay at base in every pool, and promotion is free everywhere. The time control decides how much you get to think; the multiplier decides how hard the material war hits.
rules.poolTableFootnote: Custom configurations are always available for unrated games.
rules.bounty1Para1: Captures pay both players and nobody loses time to them. You initially start with a low time, but your time grows, blundering a piece is survivable, and passive play isn't punished by the economy. A decent on-ramp, though not all its habits carry over to the other pools.
rules.bounty1Para2: Two capture-happy players can stretch a "{minutes}-minute" game to around {ceiling} real minutes.
rules.burn1Para1: The clearest version of the Burn economy. Nobody gains time from captures; every point of material that dies takes {perPoint} seconds off its owner's clock. Equal trades are gap-neutral but drain both players: a full queen trade costs each side {queenAmount} seconds, so total time on the board only ever goes down.
rules.burn1Para2: The player with the more time can afford a war of attrition; the player behind faces the Burn dilemma on every capture: can I even afford to trade? Because tolls stay at base, {burn1}'s {minutes}-minute clock keeps pressure focused entirely in the trades.
rules.burn1Rewards: Clock-aware trade selection, knowing when not to resolve tension.
rules.steal2Para1: {steal2} plays exactly like {steal1} until the first capture. Tolls and chips are identical, so the pace of quiet play is indistinguishable. But this gamemode has a C2 capture economy, a hung bishop is {bishopSwing} seconds of gap, a lost queen is {queenSwing}, in a {minutes}-minute game.
rules.steal2Para2: {steal2} is the more deterministic pool: the material war decides more, and harassment rescues less.
rules.steal1Para1: The reference game, and the pool the whole economy was tuned around. Material converts directly into time at the base rate; equal trades are gap-neutral, so only real material wins move the war.
rules.steal1Para2: The check table and the conversion bill describe {steal1} exactly as written, and every other rated pool as well, because tolls and chips stay at base. The capture table is the C1 table, which is {steal1}'s multiplier. The other pools change the clock and at least one more dial. {burn2} changes the clock, the economy and the multiplier.
rules.steal1Punishes: Hanging pieces, aimless queen play, unbudgeted endgames.
rules.burn2Para1: {burn2} plays with a {minutes}-minute clock and base tolls, so the opening is slow and you have time to think. But this gamemode has a {dial} Burn economy: nobody gains time from captures, every point of material that dies takes {perPoint} seconds off its owner's clock, and a queen trade costs each side {queenAmount} seconds that neither player gets back.
rules.burn2Para2: The player with more time can afford to trade; the player behind has to leave the tension. Once pieces start coming off, both clocks only go down.
rules.burn2Rewards: Building a clock lead before trading, leaving tension when you're behind.
rules.burn2Punishes: Opening a position you can't afford to recapture in.
rules.steal3Para1: {steal3} plays with a {minutes}-minute clock and base tolls, so you get around {perMove} seconds to think about each quiet move. But this gamemode has a {dial} capture economy: a pawn swings the gap {pawnSwing} seconds, a rook {rookSwing}, a queen {queenSwing}, which is {queenSwingShare}% of a starting clock.
rules.steal3Para2: Checks still pay {chip}s, so king harassment barely moves a gap this size. A material deficit here is close to final.
rules.steal3Rewards: Calculating captures before they happen, keeping pieces defended.
rules.steal3Punishes: Hanging a piece and expecting checks to pay it back.
rules.tempoH2: Tempo and duration: how each pool feels
rules.budgetIntro: The clock number on the pool label is not how long you get to think. Tolls drain it, Burn drains it further, Bounty refills it. Subtract the economy from the pool and divide by a typical game (~{moves} moves per player) and you get each pool's real thinking budget, here is how I currently calculate it:
rules.thinkingBudgetLi1: The toll column is a constant (~{tollDrain}s per player), because tolls never scale, the only variable drain is Burn.
rules.thinkingBudgetLi2: The ladder is monotonic: {ladder} seconds per move. Thinking time rises with the time control.
rules.thinkingBudgetLi3: Averages hide divergence in high-multiplier Steal pools, {pools} describe the game, not either player. Once material falls unevenly, the winner has more thinking time than the loser.
rules.thinkingBudgetLi4: Burn drains are estimates of typical behavior, good Burn players trade less because trades cost them, so real {burn1} and {burn2} thinking budgets drift slightly above the table.
rules.durationIntro: How long a game actually lasts depends on the total time in the system, and on the level of play, beginners usually play shorter games (~25–35 moves) with heavier material flow and rarely use their full time; advanced players (~40–50 moves) push games toward the flag or a paid-for conversion.
rules.durationLi1: Steal is zero-sum, so multipliers don't shorten the system clock. {steal2} and {steal1} have different ceilings because their time controls differ. What C2 changes is decisiveness: one blunder produces an unrecoverable gap and a fast flag.
rules.durationLi2: {burn1} runs well under the time on its label. {burn2} runs past it: advanced players who hoard material can stretch it near twenty real minutes. The beginner–advanced spread is widest in Burn, because beginners trade recklessly and collapse both clocks early.
rules.durationLi3: {bounty1} is the only pool where better play makes longer games, strong players farming bounty push past the nominal ceiling.
rules.durationLi4: {steal3} has almost no system drain, so the ceiling is nearly the full half hour, though in practice a single C4 swing usually decides matters well before the clocks run down.
rules.captureOnlyPara1: The First Edition scaled the entire economy (F-mode: captures, tolls, and chips all multiplied) in the longer pools. Playtesting exposed a flaw: the toll multiplier silently taxes thinking time. An F2 pool didn't only double the stakes, it also doubled the toll cost of every move, draining minutes of pure system time. First Edition {steal2}, marked as the careful-calculation pool, actually left less thinking time per move than {steal1}; First Edition {steal3} destroyed over five minutes of its own pool in tolls and priced a basic rook mate at four and a half minutes, so winning players routinely flagged mid-conversion.
rules.captureOnlyPara2: Capture-only scaling (C-mode) separates the two dials: the time control sets how much you think; the capture multiplier sets how hard the material war hits. Two properties follow: the check profitability table is universal (tolls and chips at base everywhere means "pawn check = +{pawnCheck}, queen check = self-financing" is true in every rated game), and the conversion bill is universal (K+Q ≈ {kq}s, K+R ≈ {kr}s, in every pool).
rules.captureOnlyPara3: F-mode still exists as a custom-game option for players who want tolls and chips scaled too.
rules.promotionFreeH3: Why promotion is free (Second Edition change)
rules.promotionFreePara: The First Edition charged time-value × 2 for the promoted piece. It was removed because the pawn already pays its way to the eighth rank in march tolls, and the new queen is instantly priced by Rule 1. A fee at the finish line taxed the same achievement a third time, and in low-clock endgames it punished the player for winning. Removing it also collapses the priced-event list to exactly three things: moves, captures, checks. The fee survives as a custom-game dial for players who miss promoting to a knight because it's all they could afford.
rules.openDialsH3: Open dials (known trade-offs, watched in playtesting)
rules.openDial1: Slow pools have weak toll pressure. With tolls fixed at base, {steal3}'s toll cost is ~{tollShare}% of the pool (vs ~{tollShareAtF4}% under old F4). Zugzwang-with-a-price-tag is a faint theme in the slow pools. If slow-pool players start shuffling for free, a hybrid setting (tolls ×2, captures ×4) is the escape hatch.
rules.openDial2: Chip scaling is deliberately off, for now. Because chips don't scale, high-multiplier pools have proportionally weaker comeback economies, making them more deterministic. If {steal2} proves to feel like merely "{steal1} but careful," scaling the chip with the capture multiplier ({scaledChip}s checks in {dial}) would restore comeback power proportional to stakes. That dial stays available.
rules.openDial3: C4 concentrates variance into single moves. A {queenSwing}-second {steal3} queen swing can be strictly unrecoverable in a way the old distributed drain never was. It's the setting most likely to produce rage-quits, and the first place to soften (C3) if it does.
rules.designFootnote: None of these are settled. Every dial above is exposed in custom games: different piece values, different tolls, F-mode, alternate capture personalities, so if you play one and it feels off, or you try a custom config that fixes something, that's the kind of feedback that's wanted.
rules.glossaryFlagfallDef: Your clock reaching zero. You lose, unless the opponent holds only a king, or a king and a single bishop or knight.
rules.glossaryFlagfallDefNoDraw: Your clock reaching zero; you lose the game.
rules.glossaryTollDef: The per-move fee for moving a piece (Rule 2). Never scales.
rules.glossaryGuardDef: The repetition rule (Rule 4) that stops time-farming.
rules.glossaryCaptureMultiplierDef: The pool dial that scales capture transfers/burns.
rules.glossaryFModeDef: Full economy scaling (captures, tolls, and chips all multiplied). Custom games only.
rules.glossaryThinkingBudgetDef: A pool's real per-move thinking time after economy drain: (pool − tolls ± economy) ÷ moves.
rules.glossarySelfFinancingDef: A queen check whose gap stays at zero. Her toll is higher than the chip, and the checked player loses the chip, so both clocks fall together. True in every pool.
rules.glossaryConversionBillDef: The total tolls required to deliver mate from a winning position. ~{kq}s for K+Q, ~{kr}s for K+R{everyPool}.
rules.glossaryDeadCapitalDef: A repeated position; its checks and captures no longer pay.

GapLadder.rungANudgeDescription: Tempo residue, a pawn changes hands, or a check lands and drains off. You won't feel this.
GapLadder.rungAnEdgeDescription: A minor piece slips, or a string of pawn checks adds up. Real, but one good trade erases it.
GapLadder.rungPressureDescription: A rook's gone missing, or a hung minor plus tempo. You're now playing defense on two fronts.
GapLadder.rungBleedingDescription: A lost queen, or a slow leak nobody stopped. A sixth of the clock, gone.
GapLadder.rungCrisisDescription: Over a quarter of the starting clock. The board might still be equal, the clock isn't.
GapLadder.rungKnockoutDescription: More than half the clock. The position doesn't matter anymore, the flag is falling.

about.metaDescription: Who invented KiriChess, when, and why: a chess variant where time is a resource. Captures, moves, and checks all add or remove time.
about.heading: About KiriChess
about.subheading: The same board. The same pieces. The same rules chess always had, except the clock is not a timer. Time is a resource: captures, moves, and checks all add or remove it.
about.repoPara: The first commit in this repository was 21 July 2026, under the working title Clockstarved. That date is the repository, not the invention. The variant was later renamed KiriChess.
about.ideaPara1: KiriChess is ordinary chess on an 8×8 board, with the usual pieces and the usual moves. No new pieces are added. The variant is the clock: it is not only a timer counting down, it is a resource that moves between the two players as the game is played.
about.ideaPara2: Captures, moves, and checks all add or remove time. Three economies, Steal, Burn, and Bounty, change who pays and who collects. The full numbers live on the <rules>rules page</rules>.
about.ideaPara3: A position that has already occurred changes no clocks, so repeating a check cannot farm time. The third time the same position appears, the game is a draw.
about.whyPara1: I started playing chess and started watching a lot of content, videos, streams, tournaments. I noticed a few different experienced players say the same thing, that they wished there were more viable variants out there. That's where KiriChess began, I started trying to come up with one myself.
about.whyPara2: My first attempt was 2v2 on a shared board with custom piece combos. But I couldn't get the math to work, balance kept breaking no matter how I adjusted it, so I dropped it. That's when I started looking at the clock instead of the pieces, and figured I could build a variant around that.
about.namePara: The name is a personal touch. KiriChess is named after my dad, whose nickname is Kiri. I preferred this over a purely mechanical description of what the game does.
about.platformPara: This site is where the variant is played. Rated games use Glicko-2 in the official pools. You can also play a bot, challenge a friend with a link, <watch>watch live games</watch>, or build an unrated custom ruleset.
about.platformPara2: Only the official pools are rated. A game against the bot, a challenge sent as a link, and a custom ruleset are unrated, so none of them move a rating. Finished games stay up to replay, and each pool has a leaderboard.
about.projectPara: I run KiriChess on my own. It is independent, free, and run at cost by one person. Supporting it never unlocks a feature; patrons get a small badge next to their name. If you want to help with server costs, there is a <donate>donate</donate> page.
about.projectPara2: Donations are one-off. The badge is a small heart beside your name. It lapses on its own, and it has no effect on pairing, ratings, or the clocks.
about.contactPara: Questions, press, and anything that is not a rules dispute: <mail>contact@kirichess.com</mail>. There is also a <discord>Discord</discord>.
about.reportPara: To report content or conduct on this site, including anything you believe is unlawful, write to the same address. Reports are read by me; there is no automated decision. You will get a reply.
about.reportInGame: If you are signed in, you can also report a player from the game. That is an extra way in, not a substitute for the email.
about.a11yPara: The board can be played from the keyboard, moves are announced to a screen reader, and the site respects reduced-motion settings. I have not yet completed a full screen-reader pass of live play, so this is not a WCAG conformance claim.
about.a11yReport: If you hit a barrier, write to <mail>contact@kirichess.com</mail>. I am one person and I will fix what is reported.
about.citePara: KiriChess by Michiel Gekiere, invented February 2026. This page is the origin record.

developers.metaDescription: Public bot API for KiriChess: scoped tokens, unrated HTTP play, and a separate bot rating pool.
developers.heading: Public / bot API
developers.subheading: Call KiriChess from your own engine. The published promise is /api/v1 only. Issue a token on your profile; the raw secret is shown once.
developers.authPara: Send Authorization: Bearer kirichess_pat_… on every request. Scopes are exactly two. A token never carries admin or 2FA claims, even if the account does. Up to 10 tokens can be active at once. A token lasts 90 days unless you choose another life between 1 and 365 days, and you can revoke it sooner from the API tokens card on your profile page.
developers.tokenShape: The value after kirichess_pat_ is 43 characters from the URL-safe base64 alphabet (A–Z, a–z, 0–9, hyphen, underscore), then 6 checksum characters. The checksum is the CRC-32 (IEEE) of those 43 characters, written as 6 base62 digits in the alphabet 0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz and padded on the left with zeros. A secret scanner can reject a string that fails that check without calling this server.
developers.scopeRead: read, identity, your games, finished replays, your open challenges, bot-pool ratings, bot seeks.
developers.scopePlay: play, create unrated games and challenges, move and resign, and join bot-pool matchmaking over the hub. Play implies read at issue time.
developers.corsPara: Your engine runs in the process that calls this API. Browser origins other than this site stay blocked; CORS is not widened for this API.
developers.playPara: POST /api/v1/games creates a solo/self-play game only, both seats are you, for exercising the engine end to end. It rejects an opponentId pointing at anyone else: matched play always goes through POST /api/v1/challenges or the bot pool. Rated measurement is opt-in: connect to the game hub with the same token and JoinQueue with an official preset (bounty1, burn1, steal1, steal2, burn2, steal3). That remaps onto bot:'{'preset'}' and never mixes with human Glicko.
developers.poolBoundaryPara: The bot pool is a courtesy to honest bot authors, not a technical barrier: a script signed in with an account's own password looks identical to a browser at the queue and lands in the human pool. Playing the human pool from a script is against the rules, whichever credential it authenticates with.
developers.hubPara: Connect to {hub}. A bot authenticates the same way as everywhere else in this API: send Authorization: Bearer kirichess_pat_… on the connection request. The first-party site puts a short-lived session JWT in the access_token query, because a browser cannot set a header on a WebSocket handshake. The server still accepts a kirichess_pat_… token in that query. Do not put one there: it is written to Fly's proxy log, Cloudflare's request log, and Sentry's captured request URL.
developers.hubMethods: Player methods: JoinQueue, SubmitMove, Resign, OfferDraw, RespondDraw and LeaveQueue. Events: MatchFound, MovePlayed, GameEnded, DrawOffered, DrawDeclined, OpponentDisconnected and OpponentReconnected. WatchChallenge and UnwatchChallenge subscribe this connection to a challenge you created; OfferRematch and AcceptRematch continue a finished game. JoinAsSpectator stays anonymous. A working loop is connect, JoinQueue, wait for MatchFound, then JoinGame(gameId) to get the current position and subscribe to that game's events before calling SubmitMove or reacting to MovePlayed; skipping JoinGame means no MovePlayed events ever arrive. Moves in a hub-matched game can also be posted over POST /api/v1/games/'{'id'}'/moves instead of the hub, if that is easier for your client.
developers.limitRead: Reads: 300 per minute per token (more generous than the human replay policy).
developers.limitCreate: Creating games and challenges: 12 per minute per token, shared by both. A signed-in browser gets 12 game creates a minute and, separately, 10 challenge creates a minute.
developers.limitMove: Moves: same numbers as a human (60 burst / 30 per second). A rejected move can still flag a game; a key must not buy a faster clock.
developers.limitAccount: Across every token on the account: 1800 requests a minute. One token's sustained move rate already sits at this ceiling.
developers.specPara: The production document is /api/v1 only. It lives at

donate.intro: KiriChess is independent, free, and run at cost by one person. Captures, moves, and checks all add or remove time. If you enjoy it, consider supporting the servers and development.
donate.whereMoneyGoesA: Right now, I am a full-time student and server upkeep comes entirely out of my own pocket. Your support helps cover these running costs, keep developing the platform and game, and allows me to expand the infrastructure for better and faster performance.
donate.patronFeaturesQ: Are some features reserved for Patrons?
